1.goal: To open on the thing the lesson is about: a conversation with three people in it, and her in none of the turns.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is fine at this point.
run: Ask when she last sat in a call where two people disagreed about material.
Take one answer and move on.
1.expected: One concrete situation, from her own week if possible.
1.support: If she talks about a call in Portuguese, that is fine — the difficulty is the same, and she will hear it in a moment.
1.challenge: Ask whether she said anything in that call, and if not, what stopped her.
1.monitoring: Whether the situation she picks is one where she stayed quiet. That is the one the lesson is for.
1.evidence: The situation she names — it is the one to come back to at the close.
1.transition: Move on when one concrete situation is on the table.

2.goal: To establish who is in the call, what it is for, and what she wants out of it.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Give her time to read the brief.
Confirm two things out loud: she is on the call, and nobody has asked her anything.
2.expected: Recognition — this is the fortnightly call she already sits in.
2.support: If the brief reads as background, ask what happens to her group if she leaves the call without the answer.
2.challenge: Ask who, of the three, she would rather not interrupt — and why that one.
2.monitoring: What the three disagree about is deliberately not said here. Do not fill it in.
2.evidence: Whether she can state what she needs from the call without rereading the brief.
2.transition: Move on when she can say what she needs to leave the call with.

3.goal: Three hypotheses, so the first listening has a purpose.
3.interaction: T–S, three open questions. Hypotheses, not answers.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Collect one answer each and move on. Do not confirm anything — the recording is what tests them.
3.expected: No right answer. Usual territory: time, difficulty, what to cut, who decides.
3.support: If she answers about meetings in general, bring it back to these three people and this unit.
3.challenge: Ask what would have to be true for her to speak up in the first two minutes.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess at all. What she predicts here is what she then listens for.
3.evidence: The third answer — what would make her speak — measured later against the stop where she actually comes in.
3.transition: Move on when three answers exist, however tentative.

4.goal: The whole call, once, for the big picture: who is there and what is at stake.
4.interaction: S listens alone, then T–S on the two questions.
run: Play once, at Normal. Then the two questions on screen. Do not replay yet.
There is no transcript on this screen, deliberately: this is the only place where the evidence is purely auditory. It becomes available on the next one.
4.expected: A planning call about one unit; three people, one of them chairing.
4.support: If she lost track of who is who, that is DATA, not a problem to fix — write it down and go on. Two of the three voices are female, and following them is part of the task.
4.challenge: Ask which of the three she would put money on as the one who decides, before hearing it again.
4.monitoring: Whether she follows the thread of the call or stops at the first turn she does not catch.
4.evidence: How much of the call survives one listening without support. It is the baseline for the block.
4.transition: Move on when both questions have an answer, even a partial one.

5.goal: Who is arguing for what — attributed, not summarized.
5.interaction: S matches on screen, then T–S with the transcript open.
run: Play again, then the matching. Check together.
The transcript is available on this screen: open it AFTER the first attempt, and use it to settle disputes by pointing at the line.
5.expected: Peter — cut the second reading text. Rachel — keep it, and move it to the start. Marta — chairs, and states no position of her own.
5.support: If an attribution will not come, play only the turn it depends on, and ask who is speaking before asking what they want.
5.challenge: Ask her to say which of the two positions is closer to what her own group needs.
5.monitoring: Marta scored as “the one who agrees”. She never states a position. Go back to the line where she restates the disagreement: chairing is not agreeing.
5.evidence: Whether she can point at a line for each attribution, or is reconstructing from impression.
5.transition: Move on when the three attributions are right and she can point at one line for each.

6.goal: For her to notice that a turn can do something other than state a position — and that one of them moves the argument off its own ground.
6.interaction: S classifies on screen, then T–S discussion.
run: She classifies the six lines, then Check.
Only then open the box with the question and let her answer before revealing.
6.expected: position — 1, 4 · proposal — 3 · reformulating someone else — 2, 6 · conceding — 5.
6.support: Ask: could the person who said this be quoted as being FOR something? If not, it is doing something else.
6.challenge: Ask her to turn one of the positions into a reformulation, keeping the same content.
6.monitoring: The line that matters is Rachel's “I am not sure we agree it is too long.” It looks like disagreement and it is a reframing — it moves the argument, and it is what she will have to do herself in the block ahead.
6.evidence: Which line she names as the one that changed the direction of the call.
6.transition: Move on when she can name one line that changed the direction of the call.

7.goal: To build the opening of a turn: name what you heard, then ask.
7.interaction: S writes notes alone, then says each opening out loud to you.
run: She writes the two lines on the left in note form.
Then she says each opening out loud, once.
Correct the ORDER inside the sentence — heard first, question second — and nothing else at this stage.
exact: If the turn opens with her own subject: “Start again, and put first the thing you heard someone say.”
If the opening will not come: “Three words to begin: I heard you say…”
7.expected: Any opening that refers to something actually said is acceptable, including forms not on the list.
7.support: If she opens with her own subject — I have a question about the writing — stop and rebuild that one sentence with her: it has to contain something someone said.
7.challenge: Ask for the same opening in a call where she has already spoken once. What changes, and what does not.
7.monitoring: Whether the thing she heard arrives before the question, or after it as a justification.
7.evidence: The two openings, and whether both are anchored in the call. They are what the production stage runs on.
7.transition: Move on when two openings have been said out loud, both anchored in the call.

8.goal: The production of the lesson. The call runs in three parts and stops after each; at each stop she decides whether to come in.
8.interaction: Role-play over the recording. You answer as Marta when she comes in.
run: Use the three Play buttons in order. After each one, wait — the silence is the decision.
When she comes in, answer as Marta, and ONCE ask back, word for word, one of the two lines below.
The first checks precision; the second forces a position. Choose ONE before the lesson.
exact: Sorry — are you asking about the text, or about the hours?
And which of the two would you go with?
8.expected: An opening anchored in something said, one checking question, and the call handed back.
8.support: The notes from the previous screen stay in view. If she starts reading them out, take them away and ask her to say it again.
8.challenge: If she comes in at the first stop, let the call run to the third and ask for a second turn that does not repeat the first.
8.monitoring: At which stop she comes in, and what the first six words are. Both go in the record.
8.evidence: The first six words of her turn, written down as she said them. They are the third field of the next screen.
8.transition: Move on when she has come in at least once and handed the call back.

9.goal: Two points from what she said, and one entry rebuilt.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the four fields together, then one replay.
run: Fill the board WITH her. Put her own opening in the third field, word for word.
The replay is ONE stop — the one where she waited longest — not the whole call.
9.expected: The point to develop is most likely the first six words of the turn.
9.support: If the entry was already clean, use the replay for the stop she let pass, not for a mistake.
9.challenge: Ask for the rebuilt opening at the speed of the call, without the notes on screen.
9.monitoring: The board starts empty. Do not pre-fill it with an error she did not make.
9.evidence: The two fields you fill here reach her Feedback tab — write them so she can act on them alone.
9.transition: Move on when the rebuilt opening has been said once, live.

10.goal: To register what was worked on, and how she felt doing it.
10.interaction: S ticks the list and answers the scale; T–S on the closing question.
run: She reads the list and ticks what she recognizes.
The scale is her perception, not your assessment — do not argue with it.
Say the homework out loud and never write it on the screen.
10.expected: Some of the lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence scale.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which line she could use in the next call she is already in.
10.challenge: Ask when the next call like this one is, and which phrase she would take into it.
10.monitoring: A low mark on “coming in without being invited”, after a call she handled well, is worth recording: it is the gap this cycle exists to close.
10.evidence: Her own confidence reading against what you saw at the three stops. Fill the post-lesson record before you close.
